content: The selection of contraceptive methods for women living with HIV requires careful consideration of the advantages and disadvantages of each method, as these vary depending on individual circumstances, perceptions, and interpretations. Evidence from systematic reviews and clinical studies has informed recommendations for contraceptive use among women with HIV, including those with asymptomatic or mild disease (WHO stage 1 or 2) and those with severe or advanced disease (WHO stage 3 or 4). Combined Hormonal Contraceptives (CHCs) Among eight studies evaluating the use of combined oral contraceptives (COCs) and HIV progression, seven found no association between COC use and disease progression, as measured by CD4 count <200 cells/mm³, initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), or mortality. However, one randomized controlled trial reported an increased risk of a composite outcome of declining CD4 count or death among COC users compared to users of copper-bearing intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs). Two prospective observational studies directly assessed the impact of hormonal contraceptives on female-to-male HIV transmission by measuring seroconversions in male partners. One study reported an elevated, though not statistically significant, risk associated with COC use, while the other found no significant association. Progestogen-Only Contraceptives (POCs) Out of six studies on progestogen-only injectable contraceptives (POIs), five found no association between POI use and HIV progression. One randomized trial, however, reported an increased risk of declining CD4 count or death among oral contraceptive (OC) users (including COCs and progestogen-only pills, POPs) compared to Cu-IUD users. This study had limitations, including significant loss to follow-up and method-switching among participants. One study found no difference in ART initiation or CD4 count between users and non-users of the levonorgestrel intrauterine device (LNG-IUD). Hormonal Contraceptives and HIV Transmission Studies indirectly assessing the effect of hormonal contraceptives on female-to-male HIV transmission by measuring genital viral shedding have yielded mixed results. Most studies found no effect of hormonal contraceptives on plasma HIV viral load. Two prospective observational studies directly assessed the impact of hormonal contraceptives on female-to-male HIV transmission. One study found a statistically significant association between injectable contraception and increased transmission risk, while another found no significant association with depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) use. Recommendations for Women with Severe or Advanced HIV (WHO Stage 3 or 4) Women with severe or advanced HIV can use combined oral contraceptives (COCs), combined injectable contraceptives (CICs), contraceptive patches and rings, progestogen-only pills (POPs), progestogen-only injectables (DMPA and NET-EN), and implants (levonorgestrel and etonogestrel) without restriction (MEC Category 1). Initiation of LNG-IUD use is generally not recommended until the illness improves to asymptomatic or mild HIV disease (WHO stage 1 or 2). However, women who already have an LNG-IUD inserted and develop severe or advanced HIV do not need to have the device removed but should be closely monitored for pelvic infections. Hormonal Contraceptives and Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Women using nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) can use all hormonal contraceptive methods without restriction. Women on ART containing efavirenz or nevirapine can generally use COCs, patches, rings, CICs, POPs, NET-EN, and implants (MEC Category 2). DMPA can be used without restriction (MEC Category 1). Newer non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), such as etravirine and rilpivirine, do not interact with hormonal contraceptives and can be used without restriction. Protease inhibitors (PIs), particularly those boosted with ritonavir, may decrease progestin levels in COCs, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. However, DMPA is not affected by PIs and can be used without restriction. Remarks Hormonal contraceptives do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. Consistent and correct use of condoms, male or female, is critical for preventing HIV transmission and protecting against other STIs. Women living with HIV should have access to comprehensive, evidence-based contraceptive information and counseling to make informed choices that align with their reproductive rights and health needs. Decision-making regarding contraceptive methods is complex and influenced by individual, societal, and cultural factors. Women using ART should discuss potential interactions between antiretroviral medications and contraceptives with their healthcare providers.
